text.content:
The Arneyan Codex | Arneyan Campaign Setting

This book holds everything a player needs to build a character and take part in play. For the world, its history and its peoples, including how long each ancestry lives and how it ages, see the Arneyan wiki.

• Levels: characters advance from 1st to 20th level. You earn Experience Points (XP); when your XP reaches the cost of a level, you spend it to gain that level (see How Levels Are Awarded). There is no training requirement and no cost.
  • Each new level grants:
    • your class's new features for that level;
    • more hit points;
    • +1 Luck.
  • Henchmen who travel with the party earn the same XP as the party, at 10 XP per level. Hirelings do not advance.

As characters rise, the scale of their stories rises with them.

TierWhat it feels like
Local Heroes (levels 1–4)You are still learning your trade. Your concerns are a village, a road or a cellar full of something nasty. A bad fight can kill you.
Heroes of the Realm (levels 5–10)You are capable adventurers with a growing name. Your deeds matter to whole regions, and rulers have started to notice you.
Masters of the Realm (levels 11–16)You are famous and powerful. You command respect, armies and fortresses, and your choices swing the fate of kingdoms.
Masters of the World (levels 17–20)You are among the most powerful beings alive. Your battles and schemes shape continents.
  • Renown (10th, 15th and 20th level). Your name grows in three steps.
    • Name (10th): your deeds are known. You gain a title, a small perk your class names, and your first follower, and from now on you may build or take a stronghold (Keeps & Kingdoms).
    • Holding (15th): your stronghold becomes your Holding. If you have none, you may found a small one now, a hall, house, shrine, camp or workshop of the kind your class describes, built as a 1st-level stronghold at the usual cost and build time (Keeps & Kingdoms). Each season it draws half the followers your class's Renown names (round down).
    • Seat (20th): your stronghold becomes your full Seat: a stronghold, tower, temple, grove, guild, school or company, as your class describes.
      • Keeps & Kingdoms says how a Seat is built and held.
      • Each season your Seat attracts followers as your class says; you choose who stays.
      • While you hold your Seat, your class grants one benefit, listed under its 20th level.

• When: the GM awards XP when the party completes a quest or reaches a goal.
  • Minimum reward: completing any quest grants at least 1 XP.
  • More for more: the GM may award more for difficulty, length, complexity or a significant achievement. Slaying a powerful adult dragon could award 2 XP or more.
  • Levelling up: every level costs 10 XP, for every class and for multiclass characters too.
    • XP beyond a level's cost carries over towards the next.
    • A single award never gives more than one level: anything past 1 short of the next level is lost.
    • Example: you begin at 1st level, so 5th level takes four fills, 40 XP in all.
  • GM's call: the GM has the final say on all XP and decides what counts as a quest. Personal goals, rumour-driven leads and structured adventures all count.
  • Any way through: beating a boss can earn a milestone, but so can sneaking past it, talking your way around it or finishing the quest some other clever way. Success counts, not the body count.

RuleIn brief
Any rolld20 + modifiers. You succeed if the total meets or beats the target (a DC, or the target's AC). Luck is the one roll-under test.
Attack rolld20 + modifier + BtH versus the target's AC. Add the same modifier to damage.
Difficulty (DC)Easy 10, Moderate 12, Hard 15, Severe 20. Interpolate between them.
Armour Class10 + armour + shield + Dexterity modifier. Higher is better.
Saving throwsd20 + attribute modifier + the greater of 1 and half your level (rounded down). Fortitude uses Constitution, Reflex uses Dexterity, Will uses Wisdom.
Spell save DC10 + the greater of 1 and half the caster's level (rounded down) + casting-stat modifier.
Natural 20 / 1On every d20 roll except initiative and Luck Checks, a 20 always succeeds and a 1 always fails. A 20 on an attack adds the maximum of the damage dice. Spells that call for a save never crit.
Advantage / DisadvantageRoll two d20 and take the higher or lower. They never stack. Situational modifiers become Advantage or Disadvantage; numerical bonuses (BtH, attributes, Luck, magic weapons, stated class and feat numbers) stay numbers.
ResistanceA flat reduction to each instance of damage. Resistance 5 takes 5 off.
Round and turnA round is 6 seconds. On your turn you get one action plus your movement. Free actions: a few words, dropping an item, and one simple object use.
InitiativeEach combatant rolls d20 + Dexterity once and keeps that place for the whole fight.
ChargeUses your action; declare it before you move. Move up to double speed in a straight line (at least 10ft) and make one melee attack with Advantage. Attacks against you have Advantage until your next turn.
Death & DyingAt 0 HP you are unconscious but stable. Below 0 you are dying and bleed 1 HP per turn until an ally spends an action and succeeds on a DC 10 Wisdom check (you cannot stabilise yourself, except through Last Chance). You die at −10 HP minus your Constitution modifier (−20 from 11th level). Last Chance: once each time you are dying, burn 1 Luck for a DC 10 Fortitude save to stabilise.
ExhaustionLevels 1 to 6, and level 6 is death. Each uninterrupted full rest removes one level.
Carrying18 slots; 20 with Strength 13 to 15, 22 with 16+, 16 with 6 or less. Ammunition is 30 per slot and coins 100 per slot. Worn armour and carried weapons count. Over the limit, speed drops by 10ft or more and you have Disadvantage on Dexterity checks and attack rolls (see Over the Limit).

These systems are covered in full in their own chapters rather than repeated here.

  • Character Creation: attributes and Method V, languages, the Luck stat, feats, skills, alignment, starting equipment and multiclassing.
  • Classes: every class, its features and its kits.
  • Spellcasting in Arneyan: how magic is resolved (saves and automatic effects), spell preparation and slots, cantrips, solo creatures, and casting in armour.
  • The Shopkeeper's Catalogue: prices and inventory slots for every weapon, armour and piece of gear.
The arithmetic under every roll in the game.

• Roll high: roll a d20, add the relevant bonus, and succeed if the total meets or beats the target DC or AC. Every roll works this way except Luck, which is roll-under (see The Luck Stat).
  • What you add:
    • Attribute check: d20 + attribute modifier (see the Arneyan Modifier Table).
    • Skill check: d20, plus your attribute modifier if you are Trained, with Advantage as well if you are a Master (see Skills (NWP)).
    • Attack: d20 + attribute modifier + Base to Hit (BtH), against AC.
    • Saving throw: d20 + saving throw bonus, against the DC (see Saving Throws below).
    • Level never adds to a plain check.
  • Natural 20 and natural 1: on every d20 roll except initiative and Luck Checks, a natural 20 always succeeds and a natural 1 always fails, whatever the modifiers or the DC.
    • On a skill or attribute check, the GM decides what a natural 1 costs the character beyond the failure.
    • A condition that states an automatic failure overrides a natural 20.
  • Situational difficulty: poison, disease, crafting, a GM-set obstacle and the like set a flat DC from the General Difficulty Tiers below. The roll total is compared with it as normal; it is never a penalty to the roll.
  • Advantage and Disadvantage: see Advantage & Disadvantage below.
  • Contested checks: when two creatures oppose each other (grappling, shoving, disarming), both roll and the higher total wins. A tie goes to the defender, or to the one resisting the change. A monster uses the attribute modifiers in its stat block, as a character does.
  • Aid: when a character can reasonably help another with a check and the GM approves, the helper gives that check Advantage. The GM decides what counts as reasonable help and may allow only one helper.
  • Rounding: round fractions down unless a rule says otherwise.
  • Elsewhere: see Character Creation for ancestry attribute bonuses and multiclassing requirements.

Whenever a check or save has a flat difficulty rather than its own formula (disease, poison, crafting, a GM-set obstacle), use this table as the DC directly.

TierDC
EasyDC 10
ModerateDC 12
HardDC 15
SevereDC 20
  • Between tiers: interpolate the DC directly.
  • Monster abilities that aren't spells (breath weapons, gazes, poison, roars and the like): the target rolls the save the ability names against the DC printed in the creature's stat block.
  • Ancestry Save DC: an ancestry or item effect that calls for a save but states no DC uses 10 + half your character level (minimum 1) + the modifier of the stated attribute.
    • If no attribute is stated: Constitution for breath, poison, bite and endurance effects; Strength for grapple, knockdown and disarm effects; Wisdom for fear and mind effects; Charisma for social and presence effects.
    • Monsters and items state their own DC.
  • Spell saves use their own formula instead (see Spellcasting in Arneyan).

A saving throw is one of three types: Fortitude, Reflex or Will.

  • Roll: d20 + your saving throw bonus. You succeed if the total meets or beats the DC.
  • Saving throw bonus: your attribute modifier + half your level (minimum 1). The attribute depends on the type:
    • Fortitude: Constitution (body, poison, disease, death).
    • Reflex: Dexterity (dodging blasts and areas).
    • Will: Wisdom (mind, charm, fear).
    • Strength, Intelligence and Charisma feed no save directly.
  • Natural 20 and natural 1: a natural 20 always succeeds and a natural 1 always fails, as with attacks and checks. A natural 20 still takes half damage from an effect that halves, and negates an effect that negates.
  • Choosing to fail: a creature may choose to fail a save against an effect it wants.
  • Spell saves use this same formula: both the caster's DC and the target's roll scale with their own level (see Spellcasting in Arneyan for the DC).
  • Class Save DC: where a class feature forces a save without stating a DC, the DC is 10 + half your class level (minimum 1) + the modifier of the class's key attribute (the higher, if it has two).
    • A manoeuvre or martial feat that forces a save uses Strength or Dexterity, whichever is higher, instead.
    • A contest keeps its stated attribute, and an effect that names its own attribute uses that.
    • Spells use the caster's spell DC (see Spellcasting in Arneyan).
  • Saving again: a spell gets a fresh save every time it is cast, and so does any ability someone chooses to use.
    • There is no general immunity: when saving against an effect protects a creature from it for a while, the entry says so.
    • An effect that deals damage, such as a burning aura, always applies.
  • Kill effects: a save against an effect that kills outright (or deals a solo its current HP) is made with Disadvantage only from a feature used once per encounter or less often.
    • This holds for Metamagic, deity powers and effects that last a minute or longer, as well as class features.
    • A feature that could apply more often gives that Disadvantage once an encounter at most.
  • Non-spell saves (poison, disease, a GM-set obstacle) use the General Difficulty Tiers DC above.
  • Which save: each save is normally tied to an attribute by the nature of the effect. Follow an effect's own entry first; spells often name their save. The table below is a guide, and the GM decides for an effect not listed.
SaveTypical Categories
FortitudeDisease, Energy Drain, Poison, Paralysis, Constriction, Petrification, Death Attack
ReflexBreath Weapon, Traps
WillArcane Magic, Illusion, Divine Magic, Confusion, Gaze Attack, Polymorph, Charm, Fear
  • Monsters use the saves printed in their stat blocks in Monsters & Treasure, whichever of Fortitude, Reflex or Will the effect calls for. An NPC built as a character saves as a PC does.

Armour Class (AC) is how hard a creature is to hit: the number an attack roll must meet or beat to land.

  • Ascending AC: higher is better. An unarmoured character has AC 10 + Dexterity modifier.
  • Building AC: base 10, plus your armour's listed bonus, plus your Dexterity modifier (limited by armour category: see Armour Categories), plus a shield bonus if carried, plus any feat or class feature that adds to AC directly (Armour Master, Shield Expert, Agile Defence and similar).
    • Armour replaces your unarmoured AC rather than adding to it.
    • A natural armour bonus from an ancestry adds to AC whether or not armour is worn.
    • Example: a Chain Mail Hauberk (+5, heavy, so no Dexterity) and a medium shield (+1) give AC 16.
  • Spell bonuses: AC and save bonuses from spells do not stack with each other: only the highest applies (the Shield spell's bonus against missiles excepted).
  • Situations: Dodge, being Prone against ranged attacks and the like give the attacker Advantage or Disadvantage rather than changing AC.
  • Stated bonuses: where a class feature or feat states a flat AC bonus, apply it as written, alongside any Advantage or Disadvantage.

• How it works: Advantage means rolling two d20 and taking the higher; Disadvantage means taking the lower.
  • Never stacks: any number of sources of the same kind gives only one extra die, so you never roll more than two dice.
  • Cancelling: if you have at least one source of each, they cancel and you roll a single d20, however many sources of each there are.
  • What becomes Advantage: situational modifiers (circumstances, manoeuvres, conditions, cover, positioning) become Advantage if favourable and Disadvantage if not. The GM makes the call.
  • What stays a number: BtH, attribute modifiers, Luck, magic weapon bonuses, and any bonus a class feature or feat states as a number. AC follows the same principle.
  • Checks outside combat: Advantage comes from the GM (the situation, including the Background Story Bonus), from Master training in a Non-Weapon Proficiency (NWP), and from ancestry, class and feat features that state it.
    • An untrained NWP check is a plain d20 with no modifier.
    • A Trained one adds the attribute modifier (or +1 if that modifier is 0 or less).
    • A Master adds the same and rolls with Advantage (see Skills (NWP)).
  • In combat: classes, ancestries, feats, manoeuvres, conditions and positioning (Charge, Dodge, Dirty Trick, flanking and the like) grant Advantage and Disadvantage exactly as written in Section III.
  • Damage rolls: Advantage never applies to damage. Where a feature would grant Advantage on damage, reroll any 1s on the weapon's damage dice once instead and keep the new result.
  • Riders: a rider is an extra effect that one of your own class, kit or feat features adds to a hit, once a round or once an encounter (an extra die, a push, a condition).
    • When two of your riders would land on the same hit, you pick one, unless one names the other.
    • A flat bonus to damage is not a rider.
    • Riders from allies, spells, brews and items always stack.

• Critical hit: a natural 20 on an attack roll always hits. Roll damage normally and add the maximum of the weapon's own damage dice (or the unarmed or natural attack's). A Versatile weapon used two-handed counts its stepped-up die as its own. A magic weapon's or an infusion's extra dice, such as a Flametongue's 1d6 fire, are rolled once and never maximised.
    • Extra dice from features and spells, such as Sneak Attack or Spellstrike, are rolled once and never maximised.
    • Spells that call for a save, such as Fireball, never score critical hits.
    • Features that widen your critical range don't stack: use the widest.
  • Critical fail: a natural 1 on an attack roll always misses, whatever the attack bonus.
    • The GM may add a minor mishap (a dropped weapon, a stumble) at no mechanical cost. A mishap comes from the environment or the enemy ("they parry you in the heat of combat"), not from making the character look incompetent.
    • A natural 1 never ends a creature's turn.
  • Luck Checks are the other way round, because low is good on a roll-under check.
    • A natural 1 is an automatic success, even against a Luck score too low to beat normally.
    • A natural 20 is an automatic failure, whatever the bonuses.
    • Ordinary saving throws are roll-over and follow the normal rule (see Saving Throws above).

• Resistance: a flat reduction to each instance of damage of that type, not a halving. Resistance 5 to fire takes 5 off any single instance of fire damage. Resistance granted without a number is Resistance 5.
  • Immunity: a creature immune to a damage type takes none of it.
  • Vulnerability: a creature vulnerable to a damage type takes double damage of that type, applied after Resistance is subtracted.
  • Per instance: Resistance, Immunity and Vulnerability all apply to a single instance of damage.
  • Damage types: slashing, piercing, bludgeoning, fire, cold, lightning, thunder, acid, poison, necrotic, radiant, psychic and force.
Rules for character creation and everyday play outside combat.

• 1st level: your Max HP (maximum Hit Points) is the maximum of your class Hit Die + your Constitution modifier (minimum 1).
  • 2nd to 10th level: each level, roll your class Hit Die and add your Constitution modifier (minimum 1 HP), or take the average instead: half the die's maximum + 1 (d4 3, d6 4, d8 5, d10 6, d12 7).
    • Reroll a result of 1 once and keep the new result, even if it is another 1.
  • 11th level on: you stop rolling. Each level gives a third of your Hit Die, rounded down (d4 +1, d6 +2, d8 +2, d10 +3, d12 +4), plus your Constitution modifier (minimum 1 HP a level). Each class lists its amount under HP beyond 10th.

pages.name: No Training Required to Level Up

text.content: You need no training to gain a level (see Advancement at the front of this book).

• The bonus: before a check, if a player relates a story or experience from their character's past that applies to the situation, the GM may grant Advantage on that roll.
  • It sticks: the player writes it on their character sheet, and it becomes a permanent part of the character's story.

Example: A player explains that long ago their father took them picking wild blueberries. From now on they have Advantage on foraging checks for blueberries.

• Common components: any common, easy-to-find component is free if the caster has a spellcasting focus (a wand, a holy symbol and the like).
  • Rare components: a rare component (the blood of a greater demon, say) must be acquired. It is consumed when the spell is cast, even if the casting fails, unless the spell says otherwise.

• What it is: some spells are marked (concentration). They last only while you keep your focus on them.
  • What you can still do: take other actions, move and cast spells that don't need concentration without breaking it.
  • It ends when:
    • you cast another concentration spell or use another concentration effect (the first ends);
    • you take damage, or are otherwise violently distracted (a storm, a rough ride), and fail a Fortitude save;
    • you are Stunned, Paralysed or Unconscious, or you die;
    • you choose to end it (no action needed).
  • The save: the DC is 10 or half the damage taken, whichever is higher. Damage from several sources at once means a separate save for each. Features such as the Elf's Keen Senses give Advantage on this save.

Inventory is tracked in slots, not weight. Check what you can carry before you buy.

  • Capacity by Strength:
StrengthSlots
6 or less16
7 to 1218
13 to 1520
16 or more22
  • What things take:
    • Standard gear: 1 slot.
    • Heavy or two-handed items: 2 to 3 slots.
    • Ammunition: 30 per slot.
    • Coins: 100 per slot.
    • Small light items (ink, quills, wax, scrolls, gems of the same tier): up to 5 per slot.
    • A Backpack provides the grid itself and takes no slot. It is usually the first thing anyone buys.
  • Worn and wielded: armour you wear, and shields and weapons you carry, all count against your slots.
  • Over the limit: while you carry more than your capacity:
    • your speed drops 10ft at 1 to 4 slots over, 20ft at 5 to 9 over, and a further 10ft for every 5 slots beyond that, to a minimum of 0, applied after anything that halves speed;
    • you have Disadvantage on Dexterity checks and attack rolls.
  • Strength changes: if your Strength changes for good (a milestone bonus, a curse, magical enhancement), check your capacity against the table again.

• Three sizes: Small, Medium and Large cover every ancestry in Veradyna. Character Creation says which ancestry is which; this section says what size does.
  • Not capacity: size never affects inventory capacity. Only Strength does (see Inventory & Carrying Capacity above).

• Stealth: Advantage on Move Silently and Stealth-related checks.
  • Escaping: Advantage on checks to escape a Grapple or the Restrained condition.
  • Heavy weapons: Disadvantage on attack rolls with weapons that have the Heavy trait, even with Strength 13 or higher.
• The baseline: no adjustment either way. No weapon Disadvantage, no Stealth bonus or penalty.

• Reach: 5ft of innate reach in melee, on top of anything the Reach weapon trait adds.
  • Heavy weapons: a Heavy weapon never gives you Disadvantage.
  • Stealth: Disadvantage on Move Silently and Stealth-related checks.
  • Tight spaces: Disadvantage on checks to fit through tight spaces or confined areas without deliberately squeezing through.
  • Space: occupies a 10ft by 10ft space on the grid.

The rules that come up during a fight: the round, initiative, movement, manoeuvres, firearms and the rest.

  • Encounter: a fight or tense scene run in rounds. "Once per encounter" abilities refresh when it ends and you take a short breather of about 10 minutes.
  • Round: 6 seconds; 10 rounds make 1 minute. Every creature takes one turn per round.

• Individual (the default): at the start of a fight each combatant rolls d20 + Dexterity modifier. Highest acts first, and the order holds for the whole encounter; it is not rerolled each round. Ties go to the higher Dexterity, then to the PCs.
  • Side-based (GM's call, for mass battles or large groups): one d20 is rolled per side instead. The side with the higher result takes its whole turn first. Reroll every round.

• Turn structure: on your turn you take one action and your movement. An action is anything that takes real effort: attack, cast a spell, use an ability or item, or some other task such as talking at length.
  • Extra attacks: Extra Attack, an off-hand weapon, Flowing Strikes and Haste each add one weapon attack, but only when you use your action to attack.
    • Casting a spell or taking any other action gives none of them. The Spellblade's War Magic and Spell Surge give exactly one attack with no extras.
    • The Swashbuckler's Flèche is also an extra attack.
    • Each martial class's Extra Attack has its own name and its own way around the Disadvantage (the Fighter's Press On, the Barbarian's Savage Swing and so on), and counts as Extra Attack.
    • Different sources add together, each as its own text says. The same source never counts twice, so Extra Attack from two classes still gives one extra attack.
    • An extra attack rolled with Disadvantage (Extra Attack, the off-hand attack, Flèche, and Flowing Strikes against the creature you just hit) keeps it: Advantage from any source never cancels it.
    • Light weapons: with a light weapon (dagger, short sword, hand axe, or any weapon the weapon table marks Light), your Extra Attack has no Disadvantage but deals only its weapon die, with no attribute modifier.
    • A Monk's unarmed blows are not extra attacks and never take this Disadvantage.

Example: A 5th-level Fighter with two weapons and Flowing Strikes attacks with the main hand, makes the extra attack (Press On) and the off-hand attack (both with Disadvantage), and once per round may add one Flowing Strikes attack after a hit.

  • Free actions: speaking a few words, dropping an item, and one simple object use per turn (drawing or sheathing a weapon, opening a door, picking something up, pulling a lever) cost no action.
    • Anything fiddly or slow costs your action.
    • Readying a shield or putting one away isn't an object use: it takes your action.
    • Nothing else is free. A class, ancestry, feat, spell or item ability uses your action, forms part of it, or answers a trigger, as its text says.
  • Ready: spend your action to name a trigger and a response (an attack, a move, a spell). When the trigger happens, you take the response at once, before the triggering creature carries on. If the trigger doesn't happen before your next turn, the action is lost.
  • Delay: instead of taking your turn, you may Delay. Once any other creature has finished its turn, you can step in, and that becomes your place in the initiative order for the rest of the encounter. Effects that trigger at the start of your turn (ongoing damage, say) still resolve at your original place.
  • Melee reach: 5ft, or 10ft with a Reach weapon, unless a size or trait says otherwise.
  • Attack of Opportunity: only a creature with a feature that grants one (Combat Reflexes, or a monster ability that says so) makes Attacks of Opportunity.
    • The feature says what provokes it. Disengaging always prevents it.
    • Being moved by someone else (a shove, a push, a throw) or teleporting never provokes one, unless the ability causing it says so.
  • Out of turn: only a feature that says so (a class, kit or feat feature, or a monster ability) can be used on another creature's turn.
    • Once per round unless it says otherwise, regained at the start of your turn. A feature that allows more says so (the Swashbuckler's Second Flourish).
    • Surprised and Incapacitated creatures can't use these.

• Moving and Dash: move up to your speed and still take your action, or spend your action to Dash and double your movement.
  • Halving: speed is halved only once, however many effects halve it.
  • Casting and moving: a spellcaster can move before or after casting a spell at no extra cost.
  • Chases: when one side flees and the other follows, the GM runs a chase (see Chases in Monsters & Treasure).
  • Difficult terrain: rubble, undergrowth, deep snow, thick mud and the like cost double movement: every foot moved counts as two.
  • Climbing, crawling and swimming: each costs double movement, as difficult terrain. You climb at normal speed with the Climb skill (NWP), and swim at normal speed with the Swimming skill (NWP) or an ancestry trait that grants a swim speed.
  • Other creatures: you can move through an ally's space, but not an enemy's.
  • Charge (action): declare it at the start of your turn, before you move.
    • Move up to double your speed in a straight line (at least 10ft) and make one melee attack, with Advantage.
    • A charge is always a single attack: no Extra Attack, off-hand attack, Haste or Flowing Strikes.
    • Until the start of your next turn, attacks against you have Advantage, even if your attack misses and even if someone attacks you first thanks to reach or a ranged weapon.
    • If you are hit before your charge attack lands, you still move and attack, but without the Advantage on your roll.

• Disengage (action): forgo your action; you provoke no Attacks of Opportunity for the rest of your turn.
  • Hide (action): make a Dexterity (Stealth) check, only while unobserved or in cover or concealment. The result sets how well you are hidden and the Search DC to find you.
    • Below 12 you are not hidden.
    • You can't Hide while running or charging, and moving faster than half your speed gives the check Disadvantage. A class feature may change this.
How hiddenHide resultYou stay hidden whileNot found bySearch DC
Partially Hidden12 to 14heavily obscured, or behind three-quarters or full coverdarkvision12
Hidden15 to 19lightly or heavily obscured, or behind any coverdarkvision and tremorsense15
Completely Hidden20 or moreas Hiddendarkvision, tremorsense, blindsight and truesight20
  • Listen: listening through a solid barrier (a door or wall) has Disadvantage. Rogues ignore this.
  • Passive awareness: 10 + Wisdom modifier. Add 5 if the creature would have Advantage on the check (Master, or a feature); take 5 if it would have Disadvantage.
    • A creature that isn't actively looking spots you if its passive awareness meets your Search DC.
    • A sense you are hidden from does not reveal you on its own.
  • Search (action): make a Wisdom check against a hidden creature's Search DC. On a success you find it, and it is no longer hidden from you.
  • Giving yourself away: a hidden creature stops being hidden when it attacks, casts a spell or makes a loud noise.
  • Unseen: an attack against a creature that can't see you has Advantage, and your attack against a creature you can't see has Disadvantage.

Surprise happens only when one side has a real chance to catch the other unaware: an ambush, a quiet approach, an attack from hiding. The GM decides whether that chance exists. Everyone then rolls initiative as normal.

  • Noticing it: before initiative, each creature on the unaware side compares its passive awareness with a DC.
    • Against hidden ambushers: the lowest Search DC among them (the noisiest gives the group away). An ambusher who isn't hidden gives the group away.
    • If they weren't hiding: a Difficulty Tiers DC (Moderate for a quiet approach, Hard for a prepared ambush).
    • A creature that meets the DC is not surprised. Features that adjust surprise checks add to its passive awareness for this.
  • The surprise round: before the first normal round, the ambushers and anyone who noticed them act in initiative order. Surprised creatures can't move, take actions or act out of turn. Then normal rounds begin and everyone acts.

A Morale Check decides whether an NPC group or monster keeps fighting or breaks (flees, surrenders or routs). The GM calls for one whenever a fight turns decisively against a non-player side.

  • When:
    • the group has taken roughly half casualties or more;
    • its leader or an especially fearsome member is slain or incapacitated;
    • it faces clearly overwhelming odds;
    • any other notable fear-inducing event (a Knight's Demoralise, a dramatic show of force and the like).
  • Morale Score: every NPC group or monster type has a Morale Score from 2 to 12, set by the GM or listed in its stat block.
    • Cowardly or disorganised creatures: 2 to 5.
    • Disciplined troops: 6 to 9.
    • Fanatics, mindless undead and the truly unshakeable: 10 to 12, and some never break.
  • The roll: 2d6. Higher than the Morale Score, the group breaks. Equal or lower, it holds until the next trigger.
  • Modifiers: a bonus or penalty "to morale" changes the Morale Score, not the roll. A bonus raises it (harder to break); a penalty lowers it (easier to break). Class features that grant a flat bonus or penalty to morale checks (such as the Knight's Favour, in Keeps & Kingdoms) apply this way.
  • Breaking: the group routs, flees, surrenders or otherwise stops being a fighting threat, as the GM judges from the situation and the creature's nature. Mindless undead, for instance, may not rout in the usual sense.

A Reaction Check sets the starting attitude of an NPC or creature whose response to the party isn't decided yet, the first time the party meets it.

  • The roll: 2d6 + the Charisma modifier of the character taking the lead.
ResultReaction
2 or lessHostile: attacks at once or calls for help
3-5Unfriendly: suspicious, uncooperative, looking for a reason to refuse
6-8Neutral: willing to listen, no particular leaning either way
9-11Friendly: favourably disposed, willing to help within reason
12+Helpful: goes out of its way to assist
  • Background Story Bonus: applies to a Reaction Check if a backstory gives a genuine link to the NPC.

• Attack and damage modifiers:
    • Melee weapons add your Strength modifier to both the attack and the damage roll (Dexterity instead for Finesse weapons).
    • Ranged weapons add Dexterity to both, except Strength-based ranged weapons such as thrown spears and heavy crossbows, which add Strength.
    • An off-hand weapon adds no modifier to damage unless a feature says so.
    • BtH is the progression in your class table.
  • Minimum damage: a hit always deals at least 1 damage after modifiers, applied before Resistance. Resistance can reduce damage to 0; Immunity always does.
  • Close quarters: a ranged attack while an enemy is within 5ft of you has Disadvantage.
  • Shooting into melee: a ranged attack against a target engaged in melee with an ally has Disadvantage.
  • Range: up to a weapon's listed range, attack normally; up to twice that range, attack with Disadvantage; beyond it, you can't attack. Where a weapon lists two ranges (60–200 ft), the second is its long range.
  • Ammunition: each attack uses one piece. After a fight you recover half the arrows, bolts and similar pieces you fired, rounded down. Bullets and shot are not recovered.
• Flanking: a creature directly opposite an ally, both engaging the same target in melee, has Advantage to hit that target.

• Attacks against it: melee attacks have Advantage; ranged attacks have Disadvantage.
  • Flying creatures: a flying creature knocked Prone isn't knocked from the air. It has Disadvantage on its next attack roll instead.
  • Standing up: costs half your movement for the round.

  • Default duration: a condition applied with no stated duration lasts 1 round.
    • A spell's, item's or monster's own duration always comes first, and so does the GM's call.
    • A stated duration is the longest a condition can last; it never removes a repeat save the condition grants.
    • A Poisoned effect from a source that deals no damage gives only the Disadvantage, for its stated duration.
  • No stacking by name: the same condition from two sources does not double up. The longer duration applies, and ending one source ends nothing else.
    • Two castings of the same spell on a target do not stack (the stronger or longer applies).
    • Nor do AC or save bonuses from items other than armour and shields: only the best AC bonus and the best save bonus apply, on top of your armour and shield. Ioun Stones are the exception.
  • Ending conditions: a condition ends when its duration runs out, on a successful repeat save where the effect allows one, or when something removes it.
    • Removers include spells such as Remove Fear, Restoration, Neutralise Poison and Dispel Magic, Smelling Salts for Stunned, and the Quick Recovery feat (see Character Creation).
    • Timed conditions count down at the end of the creature's own turn and end at 0.
    • Applying a timed condition again keeps the longer duration; it does not add.
  • Immunity: a creature immune to a condition can't be given it by any source, and ignores the condition-specific parts of an effect that would apply it.

• Half cover: attacks against the target have Disadvantage.
  • Three-quarters cover: attacks against the target have Disadvantage, and it has Advantage on Reflex saves.
  • Full cover: the target can't be targeted directly.
  • Concealment (fog, smoke, dense foliage and the like): attacks against the concealed target have Disadvantage.
  • Heavily obscured: the attacker must guess the target's square or general direction.

• When it applies: every spell takes effect on your turn, but casting leaves you exposed. If an attack or effect damages you while you cast (a Readied attack, an Attack of Opportunity, or any other response to your casting), make a Fortitude save or lose the spell and its slot.
  • The DC: 10 or half the damage taken, whichever is higher.
  • No save: if you are killed, knocked unconscious, Paralysed or Stunned while casting, the spell is lost.
  • Cantrips: damage never costs you a cantrip.

• Where it comes from: your 1st-level class and your ancestry set your allowed weapons. Levels in other classes add none.
  • Other weapons: attacking with a weapon not on your class's list is allowed, but rolled with Disadvantage and with no attribute modifier to damage.
  • Training: to gain proficiency in another weapon, train in it during downtime (see Downtime: Training & Instruction).
  • Weapon groups: every weapon belongs to a group, shown in the Group column of the weapon tables.
    • A magic weapon is in its base weapon's group. For a weapon on no table, the GM picks the closest group.
    • Proficiency stays per weapon. Groups matter only to features that name them, such as the Fighter's Weapon Training, which gives each group its own manoeuvre:
      • Bind: blades. Fighter manoeuvre: a Disarm contest.
      • Hew: chopping and crushing weapons. Fighter manoeuvre: a creature your size or smaller makes a Fortitude save or is knocked Prone.
      • Hook: reach and tangling weapons. Fighter manoeuvre: a Trip contest at the weapon's full reach.
      • Pinning Fire: missiles, firearms included. Thrown melee weapons (dagger, hand axe, spear) stay in their melee group. Fighter manoeuvre: the target has Disadvantage on its next attack roll.
      • Clinch: fist weapons. Fighter manoeuvre: a Grapple contest.
  • Improvised weapons: deal 1d4 as a base. The GM can adjust the damage die and decides whether Strength or Dexterity applies to the attack and damage.

• Exploding dice: when a firearm damage die marked (exploding) shows its highest number, roll it again and add the new result. Keep rolling for as long as it shows the highest number.
    • This applies to every die of a firearm's listed damage, including the damage a catastrophic misfire deals to the wielder, but not the half damage of a backfire.
  • Misfires: whenever you make a firearm attack roll, check the natural die against the weapon's Misfire Threshold before damage. When you roll two dice, only the die you keep is checked.
    • Within the threshold: the weapon jams. No damage is dealt, and it can't fire again until cleared, which takes rounds equal to its Reload time, on top of a normal reload.
    • A natural 1, on any firearm except a Silent Mechanism one: catastrophic failure. Roll a d6:
      • 1 to 2: the weapon is damaged and unusable until repaired;
      • 3 to 4: it backfires, dealing half its listed damage (not exploding) to the wielder;
      • 5: it is destroyed;
      • 6: it explodes, dealing its full listed damage (exploding dice apply) to the wielder and every creature within 5ft.
  • Training: any class can train in firearms.
    • Training comes from backstory (agreed with the GM at creation, at no cost) or from downtime: days equal to the firearm's reload time × 10, with a trained instructor.
    • Trained by default: characters whose 1st-level class is Gunslinger, Fighter or Ranger, and Tenor Hold dwarves of any class.
    • Untrained: Disadvantage on the attack roll, and a roll that would be a critical hit jams instead, as a misfire.
    • Untrained arcane casters also can't maintain concentration in a round they fire a firearm, until trained.
  • Where to find them: every firearm, with its price and traits, is in the Shopkeeper's Catalogue. Guns use the same Weapon Traits as other weapons.
  • Reloading: reloading uses your action for the listed number of rounds; you can still move. Quick Reload and Lightning Reload let you reload as part of the attack that fired the shot.
  • Shots: the Shots column on a firearm or repeating crossbow is how many shots it fires before it needs reloading.
  • Crossbows: a crossbow fires once a round and can't be used for Extra Attack, an off-hand attack or Flowing Strikes unless a feature says so. A heavy crossbow takes a round to reload after each shot.
    • A repeating crossbow is the exception: it can fire with every attack your action allows (Extra Attack, an off-hand attack, Flowing Strikes and the like) until its Shots run out.

• Pulling the blow: any character can deal non-lethal damage with a weapon that would normally deal lethal damage. Describe how (the flat of the blade, a chokehold, the pommel). If the GM accepts it, it works, with no penalty to the roll.
  • Tracking it: non-lethal damage is tracked apart from normal HP loss. When it equals or exceeds a target's current HP, the target falls unconscious rather than dying.
  • Healing it: non-lethal damage heals at 1 point per hour of rest, and all of it after a full rest. Magical healing removes non-lethal damage equal to the full amount it heals, even if the creature is already at full HP.
  • Unarmed strikes deal non-lethal damage by default (see Unarmed Combat & Grappling below).
  • Breaking objects: breaking, forcing or smashing an object is a Strength check against a General Difficulty Tier: a wooden door is Moderate, an iron or barred door Hard, a vault door Severe. Anything larger or sturdier is the GM's call.

• Unarmed strike: any character can make one for 1d2 + Strength modifier, always non-lethal unless a class or ancestry feature says otherwise.
    • Natural weapons such as bites, claws and horns deal lethal damage.
    • A Monk's Hand-to-Hand Combat table replaces this entirely.
  • Grappling: a contest, as for Trip and Disarm: your Strength check (d20 + Strength modifier) against the target's Strength or Dexterity check (its choice).
    • Size: you can grapple, shove or trip only a creature up to one size larger than you.
    • Winning: the target is Restrained (Disadvantage on its attacks, and attacks against it have Advantage) until it breaks free (see Restrained; for a grapple, the check is contested by the grappler's Strength).
    • Grappled casters can't perform somatic components: they can cast only spells with no S component.
  • Knocking down: grappling doesn't knock a target Prone by itself.
    • To knock a Restrained target down, spend a further attack to Overbear it (a second contest).
    • To knock someone down without grappling first, use the Trip manoeuvre instead.
  • Standing up: one creature standing over a Prone target never stops it standing up on its own turn. Being surrounded by several creatures might, at the GM's call.

• Mounting: getting on or off costs half your movement.
  • Mount size: you ride a mount of your own size or one size larger (Small on Medium, Medium on Large). Large creatures can't ride most mounts, at the GM's call.
  • A controlled mount: any domestic animal acts on your turn. It moves with your movement and can Dash or Disengage. Horses, ponies and beasts of burden don't attack; a warpony or warhorse only Tramples a Prone creature (see Mounts & Beasts of Burden in the Shopkeeper's Catalogue).
  • A war-trained mount: if it can attack (a war-trained beast with claws, tusks or a bite, or a warpony's or warhorse's Trample), it attacks as part of your action, once per round.
  • An independent mount: an intelligent mount, such as a griffon, acts on its own initiative and chooses its own actions.
  • Charging: a mounted charge uses the normal Charge rules with the mount's movement. A Lance doubles its damage dice on a charge hit (flat modifiers are not doubled).
  • Falling off: if your mount falls Prone or is killed or knocked out, you land Prone in an adjacent space. A Reflex save (DC 12) lands you on your feet instead.
  • Targeting: attackers choose whether to attack you or your mount. Area effects hit both.
  • Fear: an untrained mount makes a Will save (DC 12) against fear effects or bolts. A war-trained mount has Advantage.
  • Barding: adds its AC bonus to the mount's AC.

• Damage: 1d6 per 10ft fallen, to a maximum of 20d6. A creature that falls lands Prone.
  • Reflex save: if the faller had any real chance to react (rather than being caught completely off guard), a Reflex save halves the damage. The DC is 10 (the Easy tier), +1 for every 10ft fallen beyond the first.
• Speed: swimming costs double movement (see Movement & Charging), unless you have the Swimming skill (NWP) or an ancestry trait that grants a swim speed, in which case you swim at your full speed.

• Long jump (Strength): your Strength score ÷ 2 in feet (rounded down), with at least 10ft of run-up. Without a run-up, halve it. A running long jump never carries you further than your remaining movement for the round.
  • High jump (Strength or Dexterity, your choice): 3 + the attribute's modifier in feet, with a run-up. Without a run-up, halve it.

• Attribute drain: an effect that drains an attribute lowers its score by the stated amount, and every modifier that uses the score changes with it.
    • If your Constitution modifier changes, for any reason, recalculate your Max HP for every level you have.
    • Restoration and Lesser Restoration bring the score back.
    • Where a drain reaches 0, the GM decides the result.
  • Energy drain: never costs levels. It inflicts Exhaustion instead (see Fatigue & Exhaustion), as the Energy Drain spell does. It recovers as ordinary Exhaustion and never takes a creature above Exhaustion level 5.

• Temporary HP: lost before normal HP.
    • They don't stack: if you gain more while you have some, keep whichever total is higher.
    • They can't be healed.
    • They last until you finish a long rest unless the source says otherwise.

• 0 HP: Unconscious and incapacitated, but stable. You don't bleed.
  • Below 0 HP: you are dying, and lose 1 HP at the start of each of your turns until an ally spends an action and succeeds on a Wisdom check (DC 10, the Easy tier) to stabilise you.
    • Anyone can make this everyday check; the First Aid/Healing NWP gives Advantage on it.
    • You can't stabilise yourself, except through Last Chance below.
    • The First Aid cantrip (touch) stabilises a dying creature at its current HP, with no roll.
  • Death: you die at −10 HP minus your Constitution modifier, or at −20 HP minus it from 11th level. A negative modifier counts as 0.
    • There is no stop at 0 HP: a big enough blow can take you from standing straight past this point, so a monster's heaviest hits can kill outright.
  • Healing: healing a creature below 0 HP first sets it to 0 HP, then adds the rest.
    • Healing never raises HP above Max HP.
    • If Max HP falls below current HP, current HP falls to match, and doesn't come back when Max HP recovers.
  • Stabilised: a stabilised creature stops bleeding and stays unconscious at its current HP. After 1 hour it rises to 1 HP and wakes; healed to 1 HP or more, it wakes at once. A creature at exactly 0 HP is stable and wakes the same way.
  • Monsters and NPCs: monsters and unimportant NPCs die at 0 HP, unless the GM rules otherwise.
  • Last Chance: once each time it is dying, at the start of its turn, a dying character may burn 1 Luck to try to stabilise itself rather than waiting for an ally.
    • Roll: a Fortitude save, DC 10.
    • Success: it stops dying and is Stabilised as above, still unconscious at its current HP.
    • Failure: it keeps dying, and only an ally's Wisdom check or First Aid can stabilise it.
    • A new chance: once the character is stable, back at 0 HP or more, or dead, the next time it is dying brings a new Last Chance.
    • See The Luck Stat in Character Creation for the full Luck rules.
Everything between fights: travel, light and vision, recovery, and what the party does with its time off.

• Normal light: no penalty.
  • Dim light: Disadvantage on Perception-type checks.
  • Darkness (no light source, no darkvision): you are effectively blind. Disadvantage on your attacks, Advantage on attacks against you, and automatic failure on any check that depends on sight.
  • Darkvision (from some ancestries and spells): you see in darkness, up to its range (60ft unless the ancestry says otherwise), as if it were normal light. You see no colour, but take no penalty within that range.
  • Low-light vision: dim light counts as bright light for you, and every light source illuminates twice as far for you. It gives no sight in total darkness.
  • Magical darkness: spells such as Darkness block all sight inside them, darkvision included. Only Daylight, a higher-level light spell or True Seeing lets a creature see within.
  • Light sources (bright / dim beyond it): candle 5ft / +5ft; lamp 15ft / +30ft; torch 20ft / +20ft; lantern 30ft / +30ft; bullseye lantern 60ft cone / +60ft; Sunrod 30ft / +30ft.
    • A torch or plain candle burns for 1 hour, a lamp or lantern for 6 hours per pint of oil.
    • Prices are in the Shopkeeper's Catalogue, Illuminations.

Thin air. Above the treeline on high mountains, each day of travel before you acclimatise calls for a Fortitude save (Moderate) or 1 level of Exhaustion. A week at height acclimatises you. The Goliath's Mountain Endurance gives Advantage on it, as its trait already says.

Random encounters

  • The Encounter Check: at the start of each stretch of dangerous travel (a day's travel or a dungeon phase), one designated player rolls a d12 per day travelled or dungeon phase.

  • An 11 or 12 means the world reacts, not that a fight happens. The GM builds the encounter (see Building Encounters in Monsters & Treasure).

Dungeon phases

  • New phase: a new phase starts when the party enters a new level or section, has spent about an hour exploring the current one, or rests. The designated player makes the Encounter Check at the start of each. A loud fight, a broken door, or lingering where the residents would notice may call an extra check, at the GM's judgement.
  • The roll in a dungeon:
    • 1 to 10: nothing stirs.
    • 11: an encounter, not always a fight: residents on the move (roll a Reaction Check), a friendly or wary NPC, a rival party, a prisoner, a clue.
    • 12: a bad turn, as the dungeon wakes. The alarm is raised, reinforcements move, a guardian stirs, a way closes, water rises, the lights fail, or the dungeon's own threat advances a step.
  • The dungeon stirs: a combat, a loud noise, or the party being spotted adds one d12 to every later check in that dungeon, up to 4 dice in all; roll them all and use the highest. Friendly or peaceful encounters add nothing.
  • Calming down: for each full day the party spends away from the dungeon, remove one die; shutting down the cause (silencing the alarm, catching the runner) also removes one.
  • Rising threat: a dungeon can have its own threat that grows each time a 12 is rolled: a guardian waking, a ritual nearing its end, a rival closing in. The GM sets the steps when preparing the dungeon.
  • Encounter tables: each dungeon uses its own encounter table, from the adventure or the GM's notes.

Resting in hostile territory

  • Brief halts: they don't call for an Encounter Check unless the GM judges the location dangerous; if so, make one check and treat a result of 11 or 12 as a Hard Encounter (never Deadly).
  • A long rest in an unsecured area: the GM makes a separate, secret Encounter Check during the night to see whether the camp is found or disturbed.

Your choices

  • Combat is optional: a high roll guarantees a situation, not a fight. Talk your way out (Social Encounter), hide or flee (Skill Challenge), or deal with the situation another way (Puzzle or Roleplaying).
  • Surprise: the GM may rule on Surprise directly, instead of comparing passive awareness, from the party's own precautions: marching order, scouts, watch rotation and the like.

Ration consumption

  • Rations: rations are counted weekly. After every 7 days of travel, each character uses 7 Day's Rations (one Week's Rations pack); a shorter trip uses one a day. Each character also drinks a day's water per day. A day's water is ½ gallon: one full personal canteen.
  • Running short: may force a slower pace.
    • Without food: a character lasts 3 days + their Constitution modifier (minimum 1 day), then gains 1 level of Exhaustion for each further day.
    • Without water: a character gains 1 level of Exhaustion after one day, and another for each further day.

Falls, hunger, thirst and sleep are covered elsewhere (see Falling Damage, Ration Consumption, and Fatigue & Exhaustion). These are the rest.

Holding Your Breath & Suffocation

  • Holding your breath: 1 + Constitution modifier minutes (minimum 30 seconds).
  • Running out: you then survive a number of rounds equal to your Constitution modifier (minimum 1) before dropping to 0 HP and falling unconscious, then dying if the suffocation continues (see Death & Dying).
  • Smoke, gas, vacuum and water: work the same way. Under water you can't draw breath at all.

Swimming & Drowning

  • Swim speed: see Swimming in Section III.
  • Rough water: make a Strength check (DC 12) or make no headway that round. Heavy armour gives Disadvantage on the check, and failing it by 5 or more means you sink.
  • Fighting in water: light weapons work normally. Heavy weapons, and ranged attacks beyond half their listed range, have Disadvantage.

Sucking mud

  • It's difficult terrain.
  • A creature that ends its turn in it without having moved that turn is Restrained, until it uses its action and passes a Strength check (Moderate). The DC rises by 1 for each further round it stays stuck.

Sinking sand

  • Quicksand in a swamp, desert or riverbank.
  • A creature that steps in sinks and is Restrained.
  • Struggling free: at the end of each of its turns it makes a Strength check (Moderate; Hard in medium or heavy armour), with Disadvantage if it attacked or cast a spell that turn. A success gets it out; three failures put it under, and the Suffocation rules apply.
  • Rescue: an ally within reach, or holding a rope or pole to it, can use its action on a Strength check (Moderate) to pull it out.

Hidden drop-offs and channels

  • Wading through murky water, the creature in front makes a Wisdom check (Moderate) to spot a sudden drop.
  • On a failure it makes a Reflex save (Moderate) or plunges into deep water. Swimming & Drowning applies, with its heavy-armour Disadvantage.

Lake ice and snow crust

  • Each round, for every creature standing on the same 10ft stretch of thin ice or crust after the first, roll a d6. On a 1 it breaks.
  • Each creature on it makes a Reflex save (Moderate) to reach firm ground. On a failure it falls into the water or the drop beneath.
  • Freezing water: 1d6 cold damage at the start of each of its turns until out. Afterwards its clothes count as wet (Extreme Cold) until dried at a fire.

Extreme Heat

  • Exertion in heat: desert, forge or volcano. Each hour, make a Fortitude save (DC 10, +2 for each further hour) or gain 1 level of Exhaustion.
    • Medium and heavy armour give Disadvantage on the save.
    • You need double water each day. Without it, the water rules apply at once.
    • Resistance to fire, shade or a cooling spell removes the save.

Extreme Cold

  • Exposure: blizzard, glacier or deep winter. The same save and DC progression as heat, once per hour.
    • Warm clothing, a fire or shelter gives Advantage. An Insulated garment, Resistance to cold or a warming spell removes the save.
    • Wet clothing counts as no protection.

Fire & Smoke

  • Standing in flames: 1d6 fire damage per round. Make a Reflex save (DC 12) or catch fire (see Burning).
  • Smoke: after 1 minute in thick smoke, make a Fortitude save (DC 12) each round or become Poisoned until you breathe clean air. Smoke also counts as concealment.
  • Spreading: dry material burns easily. The GM decides how fast a fire spreads, usually 10ft a round.

Acid

  • Splash: 1d6 acid damage.
  • Immersion: 2d6 acid damage per round.
  • Gear: nonmagical metal gear exposed for a full round is ruined, and the GM decides how badly. Acid does not harm stone or glass.

Lava & Magma

  • Touching it: 4d6 fire damage per round.
  • Immersion: 10d6 fire damage per round, and you catch fire.

Rest requirements

  • A long rest (also called a full rest) is 8 hours of rest, by day or night. Its benefits come only once per 24 hours.
  • What it does, wherever it is taken: restores spent spell slots and once-per-day abilities, and ends temporary HP. Luck does not recover with rest.
  • Interruptions: the 8 hours need not be consecutive, as long as they include one unbroken block of 4 hours.

Healing during rest

  • In a safe haven (a town, inn or secure hub): after 8 hours of rest, a character rolls their largest Hit Die once on arriving, + their Constitution modifier (a negative modifier counts as 0). They regain that total each night, for that night and every consecutive night of rest during that stay.
  • Outdoors (any rest outside a safe haven): no Hit Die is rolled; regain 1 HP. With shelter (a tent, bedroll or similar comfort), regain HP equal to your Constitution modifier (minimum 1) instead.

• Sleep deprivation: a creature that goes 24 hours without a full rest makes a DC 10 Fortitude save, gaining 1 level of Exhaustion on a failure. It repeats the save every further 8 hours without rest, with the DC increasing by 2 each time.
  • Sleeping in armour: you can't take a long rest in Medium or Heavy armour. Sleeping in it staves off sleep-deprivation Exhaustion, but gives none of a long rest's benefits, including recovery from Exhaustion. Light armour is fine to sleep in.

  • Recovery: any uninterrupted full rest, wherever it is taken, removes one level of Exhaustion. Only a safe haven also gives the Hit Die healing (see Healing During Rest). A rest that is interrupted removes nothing, but takes away no progress either.
  • Long-term ailments: only downtime fully cures serious injuries, diseases and lingering curses. The GM rules the time and care needed. In a safe haven (a town, inn or stronghold) the story can fast-forward days or weeks.

Downtime occurs between quests and adventures, spent in a safe haven (a town, city, stronghold or similar).

  • Duration: at least 1 week. It may run longer after a long or hard quest; the players and the GM decide together.

Activities (choose as time allows)

  • Earn Income: A week's work (six days). Roll d20 + a relevant skill modifier: DC 10 earns 1 sp a day, DC 15 earns 3 sp, DC 20 earns 1 gp; a failure earns 3 cp a day.
  • Craft: make weapons, armour, gear or potions (see Downtime: Crafting).
  • Research: Investigate history, different topics of interest, or quest-related matters.
  • Learn New Skills: Learn a Skill (NWP) at Trained, or raise a Trained one to Master; there is no limit on how many. Trained takes 2 weeks with a teacher at 25 sp a week. Master takes 4 more weeks at 5 gp a week, with a teacher who is a Master of it. At the end, make an attribute check with the skill's attribute (DC 10 for Trained, DC 15 for Master); on a failure, train 1 more week, pay its gold and roll again.
  • Train: be taught a weapon, shield, armour or feat by a teacher (see Downtime: Training & Instruction).
  • Study a Secret: Learn what a Secret teaches, once the GM has put one in your hands; see Secrets in Monsters & Treasure.
  • Scribe & Brew: copy a spell, write a scroll, brew a potion or research a new spell (see Downtime: Scribing, Scrolls & Potions).
  • Treat Diseases: Spend 8 hours a day treating a disease, self-treated or aided: make a Wisdom check (First Aid/Healing) against the disease's DC once per day. A success cures the disease.
  • Create Forgery: Produce forged documents or merchandise for use or sale.
  • Farm: Tend to a garden and collect crops.
  • Learn Spells: Copy a spell from a book or scroll, or have a caster who knows it teach it to you. Teaching works as copying, using the teacher's book, and the teacher may name a price first; see Downtime: Scribing, Scrolls & Potions.
  • Socialise/Build a Network: Build relationships with NPCs and gain contacts to aid your goals.
  • Carouse: Spend a week and some gold in taverns and gaming houses, then roll on the Carousing table in the Shopkeeper's Catalogue.
  • Gather Information: Collect specific or low-key intelligence on ongoing topics.

Side quests

  • Limit: two active side quests at a time.
  • How: done off-screen over 2 weeks of downtime and resolved with one 2d6 roll at the end of each week; the better of the two rolls decides the result.
  • Team Size: can be done solo, with party members, or with NPCs.
  • Results: leads to rewards or consequences (minor or major, never death): 2 to 5 is a consequence, 6 to 8 a minor reward, 9 or higher a major reward.

One simple system for making anything with a crafting Skill (NWP): Blacksmithing, Weaponsmithing, Armourer, Alchemy, Carpentry, Leatherworking, Cooking, Brewing and the rest. You need the right tools and enough gold. The gold covers everything else. Scrolls, spell copying, potion brewing and spell research have their own rules in Downtime: Scribing, Scrolls & Potions, and permanent magic items follow Downtime: Making Magic Items.

  • Artificers use their own crafting rules (see the Artificer class), not this system.
  • Tools: You must have the matching Artisan's Toolkit (see Starting Equipment & Gear) for the Skill in question. No usable tools, no crafting; improvised tools impose Disadvantage.
  • Cost: pay half the item's market price (from the Shopkeeper's Catalogue, or the GM's ruling for anything not listed).
    • That one payment covers all the ordinary materials, fuel, small parts and wear on your tools. You don't track ingredients.
    • A Master of the crafting skill (see Skills (NWP)) pays a third of the market price instead of half.
    • Gems set in a piece are a material you must already own.
  • Selling: goods you craft sell to a merchant for half their list price, or for full price to a buyer who commissioned them (the GM decides whether one exists). Jewellery or art you make sells as a crafted good, never at the gem and art rate.
  • Special Materials: Only an item that needs something unusual lists it, such as dragon scale, a rare reagent or blessed silver. The gold does not cover a Special Material. You must have it in hand, which is usually an adventure of its own, before you start.
  • Time: 1 day per 25 sp of the item's value, rounded up, and never less than 1 day. A 10 gp item takes 4 days of dedicated work.
  • The Check: Make a Skill check against a DC the GM sets from the General Difficulty Tiers table: Easy for everyday goods, Hard for well-made or specialised pieces, Severe or worse for masterwork items. An untrained crafter rolls a plain d20 with no modifier, a trained one adds the attribute modifier (or +1 if that modifier is 0 or less), and a Master adds the same and rolls with Advantage (see Skills (NWP)).
  • Success: the item is completed in the estimated time.
  • Failure: the time is spent and the item is not finished. Half the gold is lost, and you may try again by paying again, or the GM may rule the half-finished work counts towards a second attempt.
  • Location matters: where you work changes the price and the pace.
    • Large towns and cities: normal cost and time. Any Special Material is a purchase or a quest away.
    • Remote villages and small settlements: the gold is 25% higher, because everything has to be fetched in, and Special Materials must be sought out.
    • Wilderness and frontier: no market, so the gold is spent on the scraps you can gather. The work takes twice as long, and the GM may call for a Survival check first.
  • Pricing the Work: Use the Shopkeeper's Catalogue price. For an item that is not listed, the GM compares it to the nearest listed item, or sets its rarity and value from the table below. The spell side of downtime. Costs and limits for books and scrolls come from Spellbooks & Scrolls in Spellcasting in Arneyan; this section says how the work is done between adventures.

  • Copy a Spell: A spellbook caster copies a spell from another book or a scroll onto their own pages. It takes 1 day and 5 gp per spell level, with no roll, and the spell must be on your class list.
  • Scribe a Scroll: Any caster who knows a spell can write it onto a scroll, up to the highest spell level they can cast. It takes 1 week and 10 gp per spell level, plus any costly components, and no more scrolls a month than the caster's casting-stat modifier (minimum 1). A cantrip scroll costs at least 1 day and 1 gp of ink and vellum. The scroll keeps your caster level and save DC (see Spellbooks & Scrolls in Spellcasting in Arneyan), and anyone can use it. Scrolls of 8th level and above can be written but are never sold.
  • Brew a Potion: Needs the Alchemy Skill (NWP) and an Alchemist's Toolkit, and follows Downtime: Crafting: you pay half the potion's market price, and the work takes 1 day per 25 sp of its value. The GM sets the DC from the General Difficulty Tiers. Only potions on the Shopkeeper's Catalogue or approved by the GM can be brewed.
  • Research a Spell: a caster who wants a spell that does not exist yet writes it up like an entry in Spellcasting in Arneyan and agrees it with the GM. The GM must approve it, sets its level, and names the class lists it joins. You can only research a spell of a level you can cast. A cantrip counts as 1st level.
  • Time and cost: 1 week and 100 gp for each spell level (a 3rd-level spell takes 3 weeks and 300 gp). The weeks can be spread over several downtime phases. Then one casting-stat check: Hard (DC 15) for 1st to 5th level, Severe (DC 20) for 6th and higher. On a failure half the gold is lost. You keep your notes: to try again, replace the lost gold and spend one more week.
  • From 4th level, something found in play: a spell of 4th level or higher also needs one thing the party finds on an adventure, never a purchase. It gives Advantage on the research check. Each kind of caster seeks it in its own way, or as suits the class (a Witch her patron, a Paladin a relic). Intelligence casters: a library or a master's notes, a lost page or a carving, a laboratory, a rare reagent. Wisdom casters: a holy relic, a shrine or a place of power, a vision sought in the wild, a sign in nature. Charisma casters: a patron's favour, an ancestor's relic or a trial of the bloodline, a performance or deed that makes the spell click.
  • Rivals: another caster may be researching the same spell (the GM's call).
  • Setting the level: compare the idea with the spells closest to it in effect and set it at their level. Real drawbacks lower it by one level in all, two at most: a casting time of 10 minutes or more, a costly or consumed component, a narrow use (one creature type, one place, one condition), or a short range. It is a level higher for a long duration with no concentration, an effect that can't be saved against, or two effects at once. Damage should sit with the spells of its level, not above them. After a session or two the GM may move the level once; if it moves beyond what you can cast, you keep the spell and cast it when you can.
  • Your name on it: the spell carries its maker's name in the world (Corwin's Frost Lantern), and others who learn it learn it by that name. The classic named spells keep their names.
  • Where the spell goes: a spellbook caster writes it into the book at no further cost. A Cleric, Druid, Paladin or Witch adds it to the list they prepare from. A Bard, Sorcerer or Warlock knows it as one extra spell, on top of their Spells Known. A caster of a class whose list it joins may copy it from the maker's book, or from a scroll the maker writes.
  • Another class's spell: you may research a spell from another class's list in your tradition (arcane, divine or nature; see Schools and Traditions in Spellcasting in Arneyan). It keeps its level and costs the same as a new spell, without the level-setting. Class-only and Path spells, and spells your class excludes, cannot be researched. You can hold no more researched spells from other lists than your casting-stat modifier (minimum 1).
  • A Metamagic spell: a caster other than a Sorcerer may hold one such spell at a time: one spell with one Metamagic option's base effect built in, as its own spell. Distant, Extended, Subtle or Flexible: one level higher than the original. Twinned, Careful, Empowered or Heightened: two levels higher. Quickened cannot be built in. Where an option counts Charisma, use your casting stat. It counts as a new spell.
  • Reskins: a reskin changes a spell's look and name, and may change its damage type among fire, cold, lightning and acid (a Fireball of cold, a Magic Missile of bees). It is not new research: 1 day and 5 gp per spell level, no check, nothing found in play. It replaces the original: you hold one version of a spell. To hold both, the second takes a place like any other spell.
  • Spell Components: when you cast a spell, you may consume one component from the table below to change that casting. Make a casting-stat check against Moderate (DC 12) plus the spell's level. On a success the change applies; on a failure the spell is cast as normal and the component is spent. One component per casting. A component that would change nothing (no save, damage or healing to change) has no effect and is not spent.

Where they come from: general components are bought (Shopkeeper's Catalogue, Rare Spell Components). Iconic components are harvested from a fresh kill like venom (Monsters & Treasure, Harvesting Venom: Alchemy or Survival, Hard, within an hour), one part from each kill, or found as treasure. A part keeps for a month, sealed. It is Very Rare and has no shop price.

More components: the GM may add components from any monster in Monsters & Treasure, using this table as the guide: one change per component, no more than a Metamagic option's base effect, or a change of this size.

  • Magic items: permanent magic items are made under Downtime: Making Magic Items, not as ordinary potions or scrolls. Artificers use their own crafting rules.
Treasure and hired help.
• Share fairly: aim for equal value among party members, favouring immediate needs; decide unique or valuable items together, openly.

• Hirelings: NPCs hired for non-adventuring tasks (labourers, artisans, messengers, scholars), paid the wages in the Shopkeeper's Catalogue.
    • They don't share treasure or gain levels, and their loyalty is bought: a bribe or a Charisma check pushes them into risks they weren't hired for.
  • Henchmen (retainers): loyal followers who go with the adventurers and share the risks.
    • Recruiting: influenced by the hiring character's Charisma and reputation, requiring a Neutral or better Reaction Check (a Neutral hire costs double pay).
    • Loyalty: called for in danger or after major events. The Loyalty score starts at the hiring character's Charisma modifier, +2 if the Reaction Check was Friendly or +4 if Helpful, and rises or falls by 1 for good or poor treatment and rewards. A Loyalty check is a d20 plus the Loyalty score against a DC the GM sets from the General Difficulty Tiers table.
    • Pay and levels: half a share of treasure by default (a full share if they take the same risks as the party, at the GM's discretion) and start at least one level below the hiring PC (minimum Level 1) and gain levels from the party's XP at 10 XP per level, never exceeding the hiring PC's level. No wage, only their share and upkeep at the party's lifestyle.
    • Running them: treat them as simplified characters with their own stats. The hiring player controls a henchman in combat; the GM does outside it.
  • Mercenaries: soldiers for guarding, patrols or battle, not dungeons. Paid monthly by type and skill, hired in groups, with morale checked as normal.
